title: Signature Mapping Creator Revenue Streams
body:
The Signature Five Rivers design is an original Signature design that pictures creator income as five rivers feeding one lake: advertising, memberships, sales, sponsorship, and services. A lake fed by one river dries when that river is dammed, while a lake fed by several survives any single drought. The design asks creators to widen the lake gradually, river by river, rather than digging all five channels at once and finishing none.

Method. To map the rivers, name each river's source audience, judge its fit to the creator's work, and open the best-fitting river first. Tend each open river with the work it demands, measure its flow in general terms without inventing figures, and open the next river only when the current ones run steadily. Review the rivers yearly, closing any that distort the work more than they feed it.

Checklist.

  • Five rivers named
  • Best-fitting river opened first
  • Each river tended with its own work
  • Next river opened only when current ones run steadily
  • Distorting rivers closed

title: Signature Pricing a Membership Tier
body:
The Signature Tier Garden is an original Signature design that grows membership tiers like garden beds: a small bed for supporters, a larger bed for members who want more, each planted only with benefits the creator can tend all year. A bed planted with benefits that wither in winter teaches members not to renew, while a bed planted within the creator's tending capacity blooms every season. The garden grows by adding beds, never by overplanting one bed.

Method. To plant the garden, list benefits the creator can deliver all year, plant them in one or two beds, and price each bed by its tending cost in time rather than by ambition. Offer a supporter path for those who want to give without taking benefits, let members pause without leaving, and review the beds yearly, replanting benefits that withered and resting beds that exhausted their keeper.

Checklist.

  • Beds planted within tending capacity
  • One or two beds only
  • Supporter path without benefits
  • Pause without leaving
  • Yearly replanting review

title: Signature Choosing Sponsors That Fit
body:
The Signature Sponsor Gate is an original Signature design that admits sponsors through a gate with three bars: genuine recommendation, audience benefit, and honest limits. A sponsor must pass all three bars to enter, and a sponsor who fails any bar waits outside however large the payment offered. The gate is kept by the creator in writing, so a tempting offer can be judged against the bars rather than against the excitement of the moment.

Method. To tend the gate, write the three bars before seeking sponsors, test every offer against them in writing, and decline offers that fail any bar with a brief, polite reason. Agree disclosure wording before accepting, keep the right to speak honestly about limits, and review admitted sponsors after each campaign, closing the gate to any whose fit proved false in practice.

Checklist.

  • Three bars: recommendation, benefit, honest limits
  • All three must pass
  • Offers tested in writing
  • Disclosure agreed before accepting
  • Failed fits closed after review

title: Signature Selling Digital Products
body:
The Signature Single Shelf design is an original Signature design for creator products: one shelf, one product at a time, finished before it is shelved. The shelf holds only complete products, each with its problem, audience, contents, and support promise written on its label, so a buyer can judge the product before buying and the creator can keep every promise on the shelf. A second product is shelved only when the first product's support is running smoothly.

Method. To stock the shelf, finish the product fully, write its label with problem, audience, contents, and support promise, and test it with a small group before shelving. Sell only what is on the shelf, support what is sold, and improve products from buyer feedback recorded on their labels, adding a new product only when the shelf's current products are well tended.

Checklist.

  • One product finished before shelving
  • Label: problem, audience, contents, support
  • Tested with a small group

title: Signature Pricing Creative Work Without Underpricing
body:
The Signature True Hours design is an original Signature design for pricing creative work: every job is priced from its true hours, counted honestly including messages, revisions, waiting, and learning, rather than from its visible making hours alone. A creator who counts true hours discovers the real price of their work, and a buyer who sees the true-hours breakdown understands the price instead of bargaining against an imagined margin. The design's honesty protects both sides of the bargain.

Method. To price by true hours, log the hours a past job truly took, including communication and revisions, and use that log to quote the next similar job. Break the quote into making, communication, revision, and expenses, so the buyer can see what they pay for, and review the log regularly, since true hours fall as skill grows and rise when a job's scope grows.

Checklist.

  • True hours include messages and revisions
  • Past logs price future quotes
  • Quote broken into making, communication, revision, expenses
  • Buyer sees what they pay for
  • Logs reviewed as skill and scope change

title: Signature Keeping Simple Income Records
body:
The Signature One Ledger design is an original Signature design for creator income: a single ledger, kept weekly, where every payment and expense becomes one line with date, person, work, and amount. The ledger is reviewed monthly against statements and quarterly for patterns, so the creator always knows which work pays and which work merely fills time. A ledger with gaps is treated as a warning, not as a finished record, until its missing lines are found.

Method. To keep the one ledger, add each payment and expense in the week it occurs, file its invoice or confirmation by job, and reconcile monthly against statements, investigating every difference before it ages. Review quarterly, asking which streams and clients sustain the work and which consume time without return, and let that review guide the next quarter's choices rather than habit alone.

Checklist.

  • Single ledger, updated weekly
  • Every line: date, person, work, amount
  • Invoices filed by job
  • Monthly reconciliation
  • Quarterly pattern review guides choices

title: Signature Audience Growth That Supports Income
body:
The Signature Returning Garden is an original Signature design for audience growth: the garden is judged not by how many pass through its gate, but by how many return to tend it. Each piece of work is a planting, and its success is measured by returning visitors, members, and buyers rather than by passing views. The gardener plants more of what brings returners and prunes what brings only passers, so the garden grows slowly but stays alive.

Method. To tend the garden, measure returning viewers alongside total viewers, learn which plantings bring returners, and plant more of those. Give each planting one clear next step, such as subscribing or joining, and treat feedback as weather: it shapes the garden, but it does not redesign it overnight. Review the garden's returning share regularly, since a garden of passers, however large, cannot feed its keeper.

Checklist.

  • Judged by returning visitors, not passing views
  • Plant more of what brings returners
  • One clear next step per planting
  • Feedback as weather, not redesign
  • Returning share reviewed regularly

title: Signature Creator Contracts: What to Read Before Signing
body:
The Signature Contract Lantern is an original Signature design that lights a contract before signing: a lantern checklist that shines on scope, ownership, payment, credit, and termination, and will not let the creator sign in the dark on any of them. Each clause is read, summarised in the creator's own words, and marked as clear, changed, or needing advice, and the lantern is complete only when no clause remains unread. A contract that cannot pass the lantern waits, however eager the client or the creator.

Method. To light the lantern, read each clause, summarise it in plain words, and mark it clear, changed, or needing advice. Negotiate changed clauses in writing, seek advice on clauses marked as needing it, and file the completed lantern with the signed contract, so the creator's understanding at signing can be shown later if the contract is disputed.

Checklist.

  • Scope, ownership, payment, credit, termination lit
  • Each clause summarised in plain words
  • Marked clear, changed, or needing advice
  • Changed clauses negotiated in writing
  • Lantern filed with the signed contract

title: Signature Handling Late or Missing Payments
body:
The Signature Payment Stair is an original Signature design that climbs payment follow-up in visible stages: a gentle step, a firm step, and a pause step, each with its own wording and its own timing. The stair is shown to the client in the contract, so no step surprises them, and the creator climbs one step at a time, never skipping from politeness to threats. A client who sees the stair in advance understands each step as the contract working, not as personal anger.

Method. To build the stair, write the three stages into the contract with their timings, send each stage's wording on its schedule, and file every step with the job's record. Pause further work at the pause step under the contract's terms, review the client's pattern before the next job, and treat a client who climbs down the stair promptly as a client worth keeping, since prompt recovery after a reminder is a good sign.

Checklist.

  • Three stages written into the contract
  • Gentle, firm, and pause steps
  • Each stage timed and worded in advance
  • Every step filed with the job
  • Client pattern reviewed before next job

title: Signature Diversifying Income So One Stream Is Not Everything
body:
The Signature Many Wells design is an original Signature design for income resilience: a creator digs several wells rather than deepening one, so no single well's failure leaves them without water. Wells are dug one at a time, each serving the same village of audience, and each well's yield is measured yearly, so a well that runs dry is noticed while other wells still flow. The design values steady water over a single spectacular spring.

Method. To dig the wells, measure the current shares, choose a second well that serves the existing audience differently, and dig it gradually while the first well still flows. Measure all wells yearly, deepen the wells that serve the audience best, and close wells that cost more tending than they yield, since a dry well kept open wastes the effort needed for flowing ones.

Checklist.

  • Wells dug one at a time
  • Each serves the same audience differently
  • Yields measured yearly
  • Dry wells noticed while others flow
  • Costly dry wells closed

title: Signature Free Versus Paid Content Balance

The field is genuinely useful on its own, not a fence with a glimpse through it, and the garden is genuinely deeper, not the field with a gate fee. Visitors who enjoy the field can see the garden's value from its description, and members who enter the garden find it deeper than the field promised.

Method. To lay out the field and garden, make the free field useful alone, make the paid garden deeper in tools, depth, or community, and describe the garden's difference honestly in the field. title: Signature Live Events and Workshops as Income
body:
The Signature Gathering Room design is an original Signature design for creator events: a room, physical or online, built for one gathering at a time, with its costs, audience, and follow-up planned before its doors open. The room's price covers its full making, its audience is the minimum that makes the gathering worthwhile, and its follow-up carries attendees to a next step, so a gathering is never a single evening that vanishes without trace. A room that cannot cover its costs waits for a better season rather than opening at a loss.

Method. To open a gathering room, price from full costs, set the minimum audience honestly, and prepare the session with its question and failure plans. Open only when the minimum is met, gather with the audience in the moment, and follow up with a recording, guide, or membership step, recording what worked for the next room. Review each room's costs and loyalty afterwards, since a room that loses money but builds lasting members may still be worth repeating within limits.

Checklist.

  • Costs, audience, follow-up planned before opening
  • Price covers full making
  • Minimum audience honestly set
  • Follow-up carries attendees onward
  • Each room reviewed for next room

title: Signature Merchandise Basics: Costs Before Profit
body:
The Signature Maker's Shelf design is an original Signature design for creator merchandise: a small shelf holding only items the audience has asked for, each priced from its full costs and stocked only to proven demand. The shelf grows one item at a time, and an item that does not earn its shelf space after its true costs is removed, however fond the creator is of it. A small shelf that earns is worth more than a large shelf that ties up money and time.

Method. To stock the maker's shelf, start with audience-requested items, price from full costs, and stock conservatively with pre-orders where possible. Fulfil orders with a plan for packing, shipping, and returns before launch, review each item's true profit after all costs, and remove items that cost more time than they earn, keeping the shelf small, honest, and sustainable.

Checklist.

  • Items audiences asked for only
  • Price from full costs
  • Stock to proven demand
  • Fulfilment planned before launch
  • Unprofitable items removed

title: Signature Creator Burnout and Sustainable Pace
body:
The Signature Keeper's Rhythm design is an original Signature design for sustainable creation: a rhythm of making, sharing, and resting, kept like a keeper's rounds rather than a sprinter's race. The rhythm includes buffer weeks, rest weeks, and variety weeks, so no single kind of work fills every week, and income is arranged so rest weeks do not empty the keeper's stores. A keeper who follows the rhythm can tend the work for years, while a sprinter exhausts the same ground in months.

Method. To keep the rhythm, set a weekly pace for ordinary weeks, hold buffer work for hard weeks, and protect rest weeks from creation and business. Diversify income so rest is affordable, announce pauses honestly to the audience, and review the rhythm quarterly, changing the pace when the work brings only obligation. Treat a missed rest week as a debt to be repaid the following week, not as a week gained.

Checklist.

  • Making, sharing, and resting in rhythm
  • Buffer work for hard weeks
  • Rest weeks protected and repaid if missed
  • Income arranged so rest is affordable
  • Rhythm reviewed quarterly

title: Signature Reviewing Monetization Yearly
body:
The Signature Harvest Review is an original Signature design for yearly monetization: a harvest in which every stream's crop is weighed, its field's condition judged, and its future decided, keep, rest, or replant. A field that yields well but exhausts its soil is rested, a field that yields little but enriches the work is kept for its enrichment, and a field that yields nothing and enriches nothing is replanted with something else. The harvest is held yearly, in the same season, so no stream escapes review by lingering between seasons.

Method. To hold the harvest, weigh each stream's income, time, and character effect from the ledger, decide keep, rest, or replant for each, and announce the decisions to affected audiences in good time. Rest fields that exhausted their keeper, replant fields that yielded nothing, and set the next harvest's date before the current harvest closes, so the rhythm of review survives the year's busiest seasons.

Checklist.

  • Every stream weighed: income, time, character
  • Decisions: keep, rest, or replant
  • Exhausting fields rested
  • Decisions announced in good time
  • Next harvest dated before closing

title: Signature Disclosure for Sponsored Creator Content
body:
The Signature Sponsor Hand is an original Signature design for sponsored creator content: a hand placed beside the title, stating sponsorship in plain words and, where the work is machine-assisted, stating the machine's role beside it. The hand is part of the title block, not an afterthought, so an audience that reads the title reads the sponsorship too, and an excerpt that carries the title carries the hand. A sponsored work without its hand is treated as unpublished, however finished it looks.

Method. To show the sponsor hand, write the sponsorship in plain words beside the title, add the machine's role beside it where applicable, and place the pair at the content's start. Keep the pair with excerpts and reposts, use platform labels in addition to the hand rather than instead of it, and review the hand's visibility on every new format, since a hand that was visible in one format may be hidden in another.

  • Hand beside the title
